title: Melting and solidifying: why salted ice melts faster and gets colder

summary.text: Sprinkle salt on ice and it melts faster, yet the bowl gets colder than plain ice. Why? In this lesson you melt and set ghee and coconut oil, run a fair test with salt, sugar and plain ice, and find out what the particles are doing. You learn why every substance has its own melting point, and why a melting solid takes in heat without getting warmer. You also meet three puzzles that are still argued about: water that stays liquid below zero, glass that has no melting point, and how melting really begins.
summary.art: Three steel bowls of ice cubes on a kitchen counter, one sprinkled with salt and wet with meltwater, with a jar of grainy ghee and a bottle of white, set coconut oil beside them.

intro.hook: On a cool December morning in Bengaluru the coconut oil in the bottle is white and hard. By lunch it is clear and pours. Nobody heated it and nobody put it in the fridge. And here is a stranger thing: sprinkle salt on ice and the ice melts faster, but the bowl gets colder. How can something melt and get colder at once?
intro.text: A solid melts at its own exact temperature, called its melting point. Ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius, coconut oil at about 24, candle wax at about 60 and iron at 1,538. You will melt and set a spoon of ghee, test what salt does to ice, and build a picture of the particles at the surface of a melting solid. Along the way you will find that some simple-looking questions are still open. Does water always freeze at 0? Is glass a solid? What is hot, and for whom?
intro.art: A child looking closely at a bottle of coconut oil that is white and solid at the bottom and clear at the top, on a sunny kitchen windowsill.

outcomes: By the end I can say what melting, solidifying and freezing are, and that a pure substance melts and freezes at the same temperature.
By the end I can explain with particles what happens when a solid melts and when a liquid solidifies.
By the end I can use melting points to explain why ghee and coconut oil are solid on cool mornings and liquid on warm afternoons.
By the end I can explain why a melting solid takes in heat without getting warmer.
By the end I can explain why salt melts ice and makes it colder, using what my own test showed.
By the end I can say why melting and solidifying are reversible changes, and what does not come back.
By the end I can describe what is not settled or not obvious: supercooled water, glass, and how melting begins.
By the end I can plan a fair test: guess with a reason, change one thing, measure, and say what the test cannot tell.

terms.meaning: Melting is a solid turning into a liquid when it takes in heat.
terms.example: A spoon of ghee turns clear and runny on a warm dosa.
terms.art: A spoon of white ghee sitting on a hot dosa, with a clear golden pool spreading from its edge.

terms.meaning: Solidifying is a liquid turning into a solid when it gives out heat. It is also called setting.
terms.example: Melted candle wax turns hard again a minute after it drips.
terms.art: A drop of clear melted wax on a steel plate, turning cloudy and hard from its edge inwards.

terms.meaning: Freezing is another word for solidifying. People use it most for water, but scientists use it for any liquid, even melted iron.
terms.example: Water freezes into ice in the freezer. Melted bronze freezes while it is still glowing red.
terms.art: An ice tray half frozen on the left and a glowing red bronze figure cooling in a broken clay mould on the right.

terms.meaning: The melting point is the temperature at which a solid melts. Each pure substance has its own.
terms.example: Ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius. Gold melts at 1,064 degrees.
terms.art: A number line of temperatures with an ice cube at 0, a coconut at 24, a candle at 60 and a gold bangle at 1,064.

terms.meaning: The freezing point is the temperature at which a liquid can turn solid. For a pure substance it is the same number as the melting point.
terms.example: Water can freeze at 0 degrees, the same temperature at which ice melts.
terms.art: A thermometer showing 0 with an arrow pointing up labelled melting and an arrow pointing down labelled freezing.

terms.meaning: A particle is a very tiny piece that a substance is made of, far too small to see.
terms.example: One small ice cube holds far more water particles than there are grains of sand on Marina Beach.
terms.art: An ice cube with a zoomed-in circle showing tiny round particles in neat rows.

terms.meaning: A pure substance is made of only one kind of particle. It melts at one exact temperature.
terms.example: Pure water and pure gold are pure substances.
terms.art: A zoomed-in circle with particles that are all the same colour and size.

terms.meaning: A mixture is two or more substances together. A mixture often melts bit by bit over a range of temperatures.
terms.example: Ghee is a mixture of many fats, so it goes soft and grainy before it turns fully clear.
terms.art: A zoomed-in circle with particles of three colours and sizes, beside a jar of grainy ghee.

terms.meaning: A reversible change is a change that can be undone, so that you get the same substance back.
terms.example: Melted coconut oil sets again in the fridge and is still coconut oil.
terms.art: Two arrows in a loop between a bowl of clear oil and a bowl of white set oil.

terms.meaning: Hidden heat is the heat a solid takes in while it melts without getting any warmer. Scientists call it latent heat.
terms.example: Ice in a tumbler of water stays at 0 degrees until the last piece has melted.
terms.art: A tumbler of ice and water with a thermometer in it reading 0, and arrows of warmth going in from the room.

terms.meaning: A supercooled liquid is colder than its freezing point but is still liquid, because freezing has not yet started.
terms.example: A bottle of very clean water can stay liquid at minus 5 degrees in the freezer, and then freeze in seconds when you knock it.
terms.art: A hand knocking a plastic bottle of water on a table, with white ice spreading down through the water from the top.

terms.meaning: A seed is the first tiny group of particles that line up in the pattern of the solid. Freezing spreads out from a seed.
terms.example: A speck of dust in water can help a seed of ice to form.
terms.art: A zoomed-in circle of loose water particles, with one small group in a neat six-sided pattern at the centre.

terms.meaning: Brine is water with a lot of salt dissolved in it. Brine freezes at a lower temperature than plain water.
terms.example: The salty meltwater in a kulfi seller's pot of ice and salt is brine.
terms.art: A clay pot packed with ice and salt, with metal kulfi cones standing in the salty water.

terms.meaning: Glass is a solid whose particles are jumbled, not in rows. Scientists call this an amorphous solid. It has no exact melting point.
terms.example: A glass bangle softens slowly when a bangle maker heats it, and can be bent into a ring.
terms.art: Two zoomed-in circles side by side: one with particles in neat rows labelled crystal, one with particles jumbled labelled glass.

terms.meaning: Casting is making an object by pouring a melted substance into a hollow shape and letting it solidify.
terms.example: Bronze figures in Swamimalai are cast by pouring melted metal into a clay mould.
terms.art: Glowing orange metal being poured from a clay pot into the hole of a clay mould.

explanations.context: This card says what melting is and why 'hot' is a different number for every substance.
explanations.definition: Melting is a solid turning into a liquid as it takes in heat. The temperature at which this happens is the melting point of that substance.
explanations.description: A solid does not melt just because it is 'hot'. It melts when it reaches its own melting point. Ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius, which feels very cold to us. Coconut oil melts at about 24 degrees, butter at about 33, candle wax at about 60, and iron at 1,538. The metal mercury melts at minus 39 degrees, so it is a liquid in every room on Earth. Chemists use the melting point like a fingerprint. Two white powders that look the same can be told apart by the temperature at which each one melts.
examples: A cube of ice melts in a tumbler of water from the tap, because tap water is warmer than 0 degrees.
A steel ladle does not melt in boiling sambar, because steel melts at about 1,400 degrees.
The metal gallium melts at about 30 degrees, so a piece of it turns liquid in a warm hand.

perspectives.explanation: Things melt when they get hot, and 'hot' means hot to our skin. This works in the kitchen, but it hides the fact that ice melting in the fridge door is the same event as iron melting in a furnace.

Every pure substance has its own melting point. Hot and cold are only words for our skin. For ice, a room at 25 degrees is far above its melting point. For iron, the same room is more than 1,500 degrees below.

perspectives.who: The Vaisheshika thinkers of ancient India (Vaisheshika Sutra 2.1.6 and 2.1.7)
perspectives.explanation: They listed ghee, lac and beeswax, and then tin, lead, iron, silver and gold, as solids that become fluid when they meet fire. They said the flowing of water is its own nature, but the flowing of ghee or gold is caused by fire. Today we would say water is only a liquid because the Earth is warm enough.

explanations.art: A long temperature line from minus 39 to 1,538 degrees with small pictures above it: a silver drop of mercury, an ice cube, a coconut, a pat of butter, a candle and a red-hot iron rod.

explanations.context: This card is about a liquid turning solid, and about a surprise: melting is dependable, but freezing can run late.
explanations.definition: Solidifying is a liquid turning into a solid as it gives out heat. The freezing point of a pure substance is the same temperature as its melting point.
explanations.description: Cool a liquid to its freezing point and it can turn solid. For water that is 0 degrees. For melted candle wax it is about 60 degrees, so wax 'freezes' on your table while it is still too hot to touch. As a liquid solidifies it gives out heat to the things around it. This is the same amount of heat it took in when it melted. At exactly the melting point, the solid and the liquid can sit together without either one winning. A tumbler of ice and water, stirred well, stays at 0 degrees.
examples: Hot ghee poured into a steel jar sets from the cold walls of the jar inwards.
Melted bronze in a mould turns solid at about 950 degrees, while it still glows red.
Fruit growers in cold countries spray water on their trees before a frosty night. As the water freezes it gives out heat, which keeps the buds at 0 degrees and no colder.

perspectives.explanation: The freezing point and the melting point are the same number, so water always freezes at 0 degrees. This is true for the balance point, where ice and water can sit together.

Ice always melts at 0 degrees, but water does not always freeze at 0. Clean, still water can be cooled several degrees below 0 and stay liquid. Freezing has to get started, and melting does not. So the melting point is the dependable number.

explanations.art: A steel jar of ghee cut open to show hard white ghee along the walls and clear liquid ghee still in the middle.

explanations.concept: What the particles do when a solid melts
explanations.context: This card gives the particle picture of melting, and says honestly which part of it scientists are still working out.
explanations.definition: In a solid the particles are held in place and shake on the spot. Heat makes them shake harder. At the melting point they shake hard enough to break out of their places and slide past each other.
explanations.description: Here is what we know so far. Pulls between the particles hold a solid together. Warming a solid makes its particles shake harder, and at the melting point the neat order breaks. The particles stay close together and still pull on each other, but now they can move past one another, so the substance flows. Cooling does the reverse: the particles slow down and the pulls lock them into place again. A substance with strong pulls between its particles, like iron, needs a high temperature to melt. A substance with weak pulls, like ice or wax, melts at a low one. The particles themselves do not melt. One water particle is the same in ice and in water. What is missing from this picture is the very first moment. Scientists do not fully agree on how and where melting starts.
examples: An ice cube melts from the outside in. The particles at the surface have fewer neighbours holding them, so they break away first.
Iron needs 1,538 degrees to melt and wax only about 60, because the pulls between iron particles are far stronger.
When water freezes, its particles lock into rings of six. That is why snowflakes have six arms.

perspectives.explanation: A solid melts when its particles shake so widely that they start to bump into their neighbours. That happens when the shaking is about one tenth of the distance between particles. This simple rule gives roughly the right melting point for many solids.

perspectives.who: Physicists who watch surfaces, from the 1980s on
perspectives.explanation: Melting does not start everywhere at once. A thin loose layer forms on the surface a little below the melting point, and at cracks and flaws inside. Melting spreads from there. A perfect crystal with no surface would be very hard to melt on time.

perspectives.who: The particle picture itself, looked at closely
perspectives.explanation: Drawings show particles as little balls. Real particles have no sharp edge, and they never stop moving, even in the coldest solid. The picture is useful and a little wrong.

explanations.art: Three zoomed-in circles in a row: particles in neat rows shaking a little, the same rows shaking hard with the outer particles breaking away, and loose particles sliding past each other.

explanations.concept: A melting solid takes in heat but does not get warmer
explanations.context: This card explains why ice water stays at 0 degrees until the last bit of ice is gone, and where the heat goes.
explanations.definition: While a pure solid melts, its temperature stays at the melting point. The heat going in is used to pull the particles out of their places, not to make them move faster. This heat is called hidden heat, or latent heat.
explanations.description: Put ice and water in a tumbler in a warm room and stir. Heat flows in from the room the whole time, but a thermometer in the tumbler stays at 0 degrees until the last piece of ice has gone. Only then does the water begin to warm. Melting takes a lot of heat. The heat needed to melt one ice cube would warm the same amount of water from 0 degrees all the way to 80 degrees. When the water freezes again, it gives the same heat back out. This is why ice is so good at keeping things cold. It takes in a great deal of heat and stays at 0 the whole time.
examples: A fish seller at Kasimedu harbour in Chennai packs fish in crushed ice. The ice takes in the heat of the day and stays at 0 degrees as long as any ice is left.
An ice cube on your palm feels as if it bites, because it takes the heat for melting from your skin.
Vaccines travel across India in boxes of ice packs. The melting ice holds the box at a steady cold temperature for many hours.

perspectives.explanation: He measured this heat first and named it latent, which means hidden. He thought of heat as an invisible fluid that soaked into the ice and hid there.

Heat is not a fluid. It is energy moving from a warmer thing to a cooler one. While ice melts, the energy goes into pulling the particles apart from their places against the pulls between them. It is stored in how the particles are arranged, and it comes back out on freezing.

explanations.art: A graph drawn on notebook paper: temperature rises, then runs flat at 0 degrees while a small picture shows ice and water together, then rises again once only water is left.

explanations.concept: Why ghee and coconut oil are solid on cool mornings
explanations.context: This card uses melting points to explain the white coconut oil and the grainy ghee on a cool morning.
explanations.definition: A substance is solid when it is colder than its melting point and liquid when it is warmer. Coconut oil melts at about 24 degrees and ghee between about 28 and 40, and the air in a kitchen moves across these numbers.
explanations.description: Most things in a kitchen have melting points far from the weather. Steel melts at about 1,400 degrees and water at 0, so a katori is always solid and water is always liquid. Coconut oil and ghee are different. Their melting points sit right inside the temperatures of an Indian day. A December night in Bengaluru or Delhi falls below 24 degrees, so coconut oil solidifies in the bottle. By afternoon the kitchen is warmer than 24 and the oil has melted. Ghee is a mixture of many fats, and each fat has its own melting point. So ghee does not melt all at once. On a mild day some of its fats are solid grains and the others are liquid oil around them. That is the grainy ghee people prize. Sesame, groundnut and mustard oils have melting points near or below 0 degrees, so they stay liquid on the shelf all year.
examples: In Chennai in May the kitchen is at 32 degrees, so coconut oil never sets on the shelf.
In Ooty or Shillong in January, coconut oil stays white and hard all day.
A spoon of ghee from the fridge melts on your tongue, because the inside of your mouth is at about 37 degrees.

perspectives.explanation: Good ghee has a grain. Cooks in many homes cool fresh ghee slowly and leave it still, because slow cooling gives large soft grains and quick cooling gives a smooth paste. They know this by practice, handed down in kitchens.

Ghee is a mixture of many fats. The fats with high melting points solidify first as crystals, and the others stay liquid around them. Slow cooling gives the crystals time to grow large. The cooks' rule and the chemists' reason describe the same thing.

A coconut palm lives where it is warm, and makes a fat that is solid at 24 degrees. Mustard and flax grow through cold winters, and make oils that stay liquid near 0. Researchers have found this pattern in many seed oils, and think this helps seeds to use their stored oil in the weather they sprout in.

explanations.art: Two pictures of the same kitchen shelf: at 7 in the morning with a thermometer showing 19 degrees and white set coconut oil, and at 2 in the afternoon showing 30 degrees and clear oil.

explanations.concept: Why salt melts ice, and makes it colder
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the salt test: the salted ice melted fastest and its bowl was the coldest.
explanations.definition: Salt dissolved in water lowers the temperature at which the water can freeze. Ice touching salty water melts even below 0 degrees, and the melting takes heat from the ice and everything around it.
explanations.description: Here is a simplified picture, and it is the one chemists use to explain this. At the surface of wet ice two things happen all the time. Water particles break away from the ice into the liquid, and water particles from the liquid join the ice. At 0 degrees the two happen equally fast, so the ice neither grows nor shrinks. Now add salt. It dissolves in the thin layer of water on the ice. Some of the particles that touch the ice are now salt, so fewer water particles join the ice each second. Just as many break away as before. More leave than join, so the ice melts. Breaking away takes heat. No one is heating the bowl, so the heat comes from the ice, the salty water and the bowl. They all get colder. The cooling goes on until leaving and joining are equal again, at a new, lower temperature. With plenty of salt this can be as low as minus 21 degrees. A colder bowl also draws heat from the warm room faster, which melts the ice faster still. Sugar does the same, but a spoon of sugar has about ten times fewer particles than a spoon of salt, because each sugar particle is much bigger. So sugar does less.
examples: A kulfi seller packs the metal cones in a pot of ice and salt. Plain ice at 0 degrees would only chill the sweet milk. Ice and salt at minus 15 freezes it.
The sea around Antarctica is salty, so it stays liquid down to about minus 2 degrees.
In cold countries salt is spread on icy roads. It stops working when the road is colder than about minus 21 degrees.

perspectives.explanation: Salt must be heating the ice, because the ice melts. Touching the bowl shows this cannot be right. The salted bowl is the coldest one.

Salt gives no heat. It tips the balance between particles leaving the ice and particles joining it. Any substance that dissolves in the water does this, and what matters most is how many particles it adds.

People froze sweet milk with ice and salt long before anyone drew a particle. In a home with no freezer, this is still the way to make kulfi. The practice came first and the explanation came centuries later.

explanations.art: A zoomed-in view of the wet surface of an ice cube: water particles leaving the neat rows of ice, a few returning, and larger salt particles in the liquid getting in the way of the returning ones.

explanations.context: This card is about water that is colder than its freezing point and still liquid, and about living beings who start or stop ice on purpose.
explanations.definition: A supercooled liquid has been cooled below its freezing point without turning solid. It stays liquid until a first seed of the solid forms. Then it freezes very fast.
explanations.description: To freeze, some water particles must first line up in the pattern of ice. This first tiny group is called a seed. Just below 0 degrees a small seed is more likely to break up than to grow. A speck of dust, a scratch on the bottle or a hard knock helps a seed get big enough to grow. In very clean, still water there is nothing to help, so the water can stay liquid well below 0. Tiny drops of pure water in high clouds stay liquid down to about minus 40 degrees. When supercooled water does freeze, it gives out its hidden heat and warms back up to 0. Only part of it turns to ice, so you get slush. A solid is very hard to heat above its melting point, because its surface is always ready to melt. So ice melts on time, but water can freeze late.
examples: A sealed bottle of filtered water left still in a freezer for about two hours can be liquid at minus 5 degrees. A knock on the table turns it to slush in seconds.
Many clouds over the Himalaya are made of supercooled drops. When they touch an aeroplane wing they freeze onto it at once.
Rain that freezes the moment it lands on a cold road is supercooled rain.

perspectives.explanation: Supercooling shows that freezing needs a start. It is a matter of chance when the first seed forms, so nobody can say the exact second a given bottle will freeze.

perspectives.who: The bacteria Pseudomonas syringae, who live on leaves
perspectives.explanation: They build a protein on their outer skin that holds water particles in the pattern of ice. With this seed, water freezes at about minus 2 degrees. Leroy Maki and others reported this in 1974. Researchers think the frost opens the leaf, so that the bacteria can feed.

perspectives.who: Fish of the Antarctic sea, and wood frogs of North America
perspectives.explanation: The fish make proteins that cling to tiny ice seeds and stop them from growing, as Arthur DeVries found in the 1960s. Wood frogs do the opposite. They let ice form between their cells in winter and thaw alive in spring, as Janet Storey and Kenneth Storey have studied for many years.

explanations.art: A clear plastic bottle of water held at an angle, the top third white with needle-like ice spreading downwards into clear water.

explanations.concept: Glass: a solid with no melting point
explanations.context: This card is about glass, which does not fit neatly into 'solid' or 'liquid', and about what scientists still argue over.
explanations.definition: Glass is a hard material whose particles are jumbled, as in a liquid, but stuck in place, as in a solid. It has no exact melting point. It softens little by little as it is heated.
explanations.description: Window glass is made by melting sand with soda and lime at about 1,500 degrees. As it cools it does not suddenly freeze at one temperature. It gets thicker and slower, like honey in a fridge, until its particles can no longer move past each other. They are stuck wherever they were, with no neat rows. Heat it again and it does not melt at a point. It softens slowly, which is why a bangle maker can bend it and a glass blower can blow it. Butter, chocolate and tar soften slowly too, but for a different reason: they are mixtures. Tar on a road in May shows the same puzzle. It looks solid, yet over weeks it flows. In an experiment begun in 1927 in Australia, a lump of pitch in a funnel has dripped only nine drops.
examples: A glass bangle maker in Firozabad softens a glass rod in a flame and winds it into rings.
A road in Hyderabad in May shows tyre marks in the tar by evening.
Sugar syrup cooled quickly sets into clear hard candy, which is a glass made of sugar. Cooled slowly, it forms sugar crystals.

perspectives.explanation: Glass is really a liquid that flows too slowly to see. The proof given is that very old window panes are thicker at the bottom.

perspectives.who: Most materials scientists, such as Edgar Zanotto
perspectives.explanation: Glass is a solid. It keeps its shape and breaks like a solid. In 1998 Zanotto worked out that a window pane would need far longer than the age of the universe to flow by an amount you could see. Old panes are uneven because of the way they were made.

perspectives.who: Physicists who study the glass change
perspectives.explanation: The honest answer depends on how long you watch. Over a day, pitch is a solid. Over ten years, it is a liquid. Nobody has yet shown whether glass is a true state of matter of its own, or a liquid that has simply become too slow to move.

explanations.art: A woman bangle maker holding a glowing soft glass rod over a small furnace and winding it around an iron rod, with finished bangles beside her.

explanations.concept: Melting and solidifying are reversible changes
explanations.context: This card says why melting can be undone, and looks closely at what does and does not come back.
explanations.definition: A reversible change is one that can be undone. Melting is undone by solidifying. The substance is the same before and after, and none of it is lost.
explanations.description: Melt a block of ice and freeze the water again, and you have the same water. No new substance was made, and the weight is the same. This is different from burning or cooking. A burnt matchstick or a cooked dosa cannot be turned back. Because melting is reversible, people can use the same metal, wax and glass again and again. Old steel, broken bangles and gold ornaments are melted and made into new things. Look closer, though, and one thing does not come back by itself: the shape and the inner pattern. A melted ice sculpture freezes into a block, not a sculpture. Melted and re-set chocolate turns dull and crumbly, because its fat crystals have formed in a different pattern.
examples: A goldsmith in Thrissur melts an old bangle and casts the same gold as a pair of earrings.
Candle makers collect the drips and stubs of old candles and melt them into new candles.
Weigh a closed bottle of ice, let it melt and weigh it again. The weight is the same.

perspectives.explanation: Melting and solidifying are fully reversible. You get the same substance back, in the same amount. This is correct, and it is what makes recycling possible.

perspectives.who: Sculptors, chocolate makers and metal workers
perspectives.explanation: The substance comes back but the form does not. How a liquid is cooled decides the grain, the shine and the strength of the solid. Fast-cooled and slow-cooled steel are the same substance and behave very differently.

explanations.art: A loop of four pictures: a gold bangle, a small pot of glowing liquid gold, a mould being filled, and a pair of gold earrings.

explanations.concept: Melting is not the same as dissolving
explanations.context: This card separates two changes that people often mix up, because in both a solid seems to disappear into a liquid.
explanations.definition: Melting needs one substance and heat: the solid becomes its own liquid. Dissolving needs two substances: a solid spreads out, particle by particle, into a different liquid.
explanations.description: Sugar stirred into cold water does not melt. It dissolves. The water is far colder than the temperature at which sugar turns liquid by heat. An ice cube in a tumbler of water melts, because it turns into its own liquid, water. To check which one you are seeing, ask two questions. How many substances are there? Did the solid need to reach its own melting point? Salt on ice is a special case in which both happen together. The salt dissolves in the wet layer on the ice, and that makes the ice melt.
examples: Jaggery in hot tea is dissolving. A lump of jaggery heated alone in a pan softens and turns liquid.
Butter on a hot dosa is melting. Nothing else is needed but heat.
Salt stirred into rasam is dissolving. Salt alone melts only at 801 degrees.
explanations.one_view: This is a definition that scientists agreed on so that the two words always mean two different things, and no one disputes it. The one tricky case, salt on ice, has its own card.
explanations.art: Two tumblers side by side: an ice cube shrinking in plain water labelled melting, and a spoon of sugar vanishing into water labelled dissolving.

explanations.concept: Shrink or grow: what happens to the size
explanations.context: This card is about a liquid changing size as it turns solid, and why water is one of the few that grows.
explanations.definition: Most liquids shrink a little when they solidify, because their particles pack closer together. Water does the opposite and grows by about one eleventh when it freezes.
explanations.description: Look at a jar of set ghee or a candle. The top has a dip in the middle. The liquid shrank as it solidified, and the last part to set sank inwards. Solid ghee is packed tighter than melted ghee, so a lump of solid ghee sinks in melted ghee. Water is different. Its particles lock into open rings of six, and these take up more room than the loose particles of liquid water. So ice takes up more room than the water it came from, and ice floats. A few other substances grow on freezing as water does, such as the metals gallium and bismuth.
examples: Ice cubes in a tray have a small bump on top, pushed up as the water grew.
A full, closed bottle of water left in the freezer can bulge or split.
A lake in Ladakh freezes from the top, because ice floats. The fish live in the liquid water underneath.
explanations.one_view: Anyone can measure this with a marked tumbler and get the same result, and no group of scientists reads it differently. The reason, the open ring pattern of ice, is seen directly with X-rays.
explanations.art: Two plastic tumblers with a marker line on each: one with ice bulging above the line, one with set coconut oil dipping below the line.

explanations.context: This card is about solids that turn straight into a gas, and why 'this solid does not melt' is only true at the air pressure we live in.
explanations.definition: Some solids change directly into a gas without becoming a liquid first. This change is called sublimation.
explanations.description: A camphor tablet left in an open box gets smaller each week and leaves no puddle. Its particles leave the solid one by one and go into the air, which is why you can smell it. Naphthalene balls in a cupboard do the same. Solid carbon dioxide, called dry ice, turns to gas at minus 78 degrees and never forms a liquid in the open air. But this is not the whole story. Squeeze carbon dioxide hard enough, as inside a fire extinguisher, and it is a liquid. So whether a solid melts or skips the liquid depends on the pressure around it, as well as on the temperature.
examples: Camphor tablets kept for puja slowly vanish from an open tin.
Dry ice packed around ice cream for a long journey gives off white mist and leaves the box dry.
Frozen clothes on a line in Kargil dry out, because the ice in them slowly turns straight to vapour.

perspectives.explanation: Camphor and dry ice are solids that do not melt. This is what we see in the open air.

Every one of these substances has a liquid form. We do not see it, because the air on Earth does not press hard enough. Deep inside the Earth the pressure is so great that the iron core is solid, though it is about as hot as the surface of the Sun. Inge Lehmann found this solid inner core in 1936 from earthquake waves.

explanations.art: A tin of white camphor tablets with one tablet much smaller than the rest, and faint dotted lines rising from it into the air.

agreed.text: Thermometers all over the world are set using melting and freezing points.
agreed.evidence: The world's temperature scale, agreed in 1990, is fixed by a list of exact points. Among them are the melting point of gallium (29.7646 degrees) and the freezing points of tin, zinc, silver and gold. A laboratory in Delhi and one in Paris get the same numbers.

agreed.text: Nothing is lost or gained in weight when a substance melts or solidifies.
agreed.evidence: A sealed bottle of ice weighs the same after the ice has melted. Careful weighings have shown this since the 1700s, and you can check it on a kitchen scale.

agreed.text: Pressing on a solid changes its melting point.
agreed.evidence: Earthquake waves pass through the centre of the Earth in a way that only a solid allows. Inge Lehmann showed this in 1936. The iron there is about as hot as the surface of the Sun, but the huge pressure keeps it solid.

agreed.text: Something dissolved in a liquid lowers its freezing point, and the number of dissolved particles matters most.
agreed.evidence: Measured since the 1880s by François-Marie Raoult and many others. Sea water freezes at about minus 2 degrees. Water with as much salt as it can hold freezes at about minus 21.

agreed.text: Very small pieces of a solid melt at a lower temperature than a big piece.
agreed.evidence: In 1976 Philippe Buffat and Jean-Pierre Borel measured specks of gold a few millionths of a millimetre across. They melted hundreds of degrees below 1,064. In a tiny speck most particles are at the surface, where they are held less firmly.

challenging.context: This card is about the story that old church windows prove glass is a slow liquid.
challenging.claim: Old window panes are thicker at the bottom because the glass has slowly flowed down over hundreds of years.
challenging.who: A popular belief, repeated in some books and by many tour guides
challenging.for: Many panes in buildings 500 or more years old really are thicker along one edge, and glass does have jumbled particles like a liquid.
challenging.against: Edgar Zanotto worked out in 1998 that such a flow would take far longer than the age of the universe. Old panes were made by spinning or blowing and came out uneven, and some are fitted with the thick edge at the top. Roman glass 2,000 years old and old telescope lenses have kept their shape.

challenging.context: This card is about whether glass is a real state of matter of its own. Physicists have not settled it.
challenging.claim: Glass is not a true solid state. It is a liquid that has become too slow to move, and nothing sudden happens when it 'sets'.
challenging.who: One group of physicists who study glass. Another group holds the opposite.
challenging.for: No sharp change is seen when a liquid turns to glass. The slowing is smooth, and a glass cooled more slowly sets at a slightly lower temperature, which a true freezing point would not do.
challenging.against: Other physicists think a real hidden change lies underneath, and that we never reach it because the liquid becomes too slow first. Some computer models and experiments on very old amber and very stable glasses point this way.

challenging.context: This card looks again at the plain statement that each substance has one fixed melting point.
challenging.claim: The melting point of a substance is not one fixed number. It changes with pressure, with the size of the piece and with tiny amounts of other substances.
challenging.who: Physicists and chemists who measure melting very carefully
challenging.for: Specks of gold a few particles wide melt hundreds of degrees lower than a gold bangle. The Earth's iron core is solid at more than 5,000 degrees because of pressure. A pinch of salt lowers the melting point of ice.
challenging.against: For a pure substance, in pieces big enough to see, at the air pressure we live in, the melting point is so steady that the world's thermometers are set by it. The fixed number is true, as long as you say the conditions.

challenging.context: This card is about a surprise in the kitchen: sugar may not truly melt.
challenging.claim: Table sugar has no true melting point. When heated it starts to break down into new substances before it melts, and that is what caramel is.
challenging.who: Shelly Schmidt and her group at the University of Illinois, in 2011
challenging.for: They found that the temperature at which sugar turns liquid depends on how fast it is heated. Heated very slowly, it turned liquid at a much lower temperature. A true melting point does not change with the speed of heating.
challenging.against: Yrjö Roos and other food scientists answered that sugar does melt, at about 186 degrees, and that it also breaks down at the same time. They say the two changes overlap and can be told apart.

challenging.context: This card is about very cold liquid water, where some scientists think water may come in two liquid forms.
challenging.claim: Deeply supercooled water can exist as two different liquids, one more tightly packed than the other.
challenging.who: Peter Poole, Francesco Sciortino, Ulrich Essmann and Eugene Stanley proposed it in 1992
challenging.for: Computer models of water show two liquids. In 2020 a team led by Kyung Hwan Kim and Anders Nilsson used very fast X-ray flashes and reported seeing water switch between them, near minus 70 degrees.
challenging.against: Water this cold freezes in less than a thousandth of a second, so the measurements are very hard to make and to repeat. Some scientists think the signs can be explained by tiny ice crystals forming.

big_questions.q: An ice cube in ice-cold water looks as if nothing is happening. If particles are leaving and joining it all the time, is it the same ice cube after an hour?
big_questions.hint: Think of a queue at a ration shop that stays the same length while people join and leave. Is it the same queue?

big_questions.q: One water particle alone cannot be ice or water. How many particles do you think it takes before the words 'solid' and 'liquid' start to mean something?
big_questions.hint: Can one person be a crowd? Can two? Where would you draw the line, and does a sharp line exist?

big_questions.q: If pitch is a solid when you watch it for a day and a liquid when you watch it for ten years, which one is it really?
big_questions.hint: Think about a mountain. Does it look the same to you as it would to someone who could watch for a million years?

big_questions.q: For melted bronze, 900 degrees is cold enough to freeze. For ice, your hand is hot enough to melt. So what do 'hot' and 'cold' mean, and for whom?
big_questions.hint: Whose skin, or whose particles, are we asking? Try saying 'hot' from the point of view of an ice cube.

big_questions.q: The Earth is at a temperature where water can be ice, liquid and vapour all at once. What would life be like on a world where water was only ever ice?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a liquid lets living beings do that a solid does not. Then ask whether another liquid could do the job.

big_questions.q: A goldsmith melts your great-grandmother's bangle and makes a ring. Is the ring her bangle?
big_questions.hint: What was the bangle: the gold, the shape, or the memory? Which of these went through the melting?

big_questions.q: Your body keeps some of its fats just melted and its bones solid, every second, without you deciding. Who or what is keeping that balance?
big_questions.hint: Notice your warm skin on a cold morning. Where does the warmth come from, and what would happen to you without it?

how_we_found_out.context: Does water always freeze at its freezing point? This card tells how an instrument maker found, by accident, that it does not.
how_we_found_out.story: Three hundred years ago, people who studied nature were sure of one thing about water. Cool it to its freezing point and it turns to ice. This fitted everything they saw in ponds and buckets. Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit made thermometers in Amsterdam. On a bitterly cold night in 1721 he left a sealed glass ball of clean water outside. In the morning his thermometer showed that the air was far below the freezing point. But the water in the ball was still liquid. When he disturbed it, thin plates of ice shot through the water in a moment. He tried again and again, and reported it to the Royal Society in London in 1724. Water could be colder than its freezing point and still be liquid. Freezing needed something to start it. He also saw that a mixture of ice and water always came back to the same temperature. So the dependable point was the one where ice melts. That is why later thermometer makers, such as Anders Celsius in 1742, used melting ice to mark their scales.
how_we_found_out.who: Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit, a maker of thermometers and other instruments
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought water always turns to ice the moment it is cooled to its freezing point. Fahrenheit found clean, still water liquid at a temperature far below that. Freezing has to be started by a seed or a knock, but melting ice always holds the same temperature.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in a long coat and wig on a snowy doorstep in the early morning, holding up a small sealed glass ball of water, with ice plates starting to spread inside it.

story.title: The Lamp That Became a Dancer
text: Thenmozhi was ten, and she had grown up with the sound of hammers. Her aunt, Valli Chithi, made bronze figures in a workshop in Swamimalai, near the Kaveri river in Tamil Nadu.

In the May holidays her cousin Kabir came from Delhi. He was eleven and had never seen metal poured. 'Come before the sun is up tomorrow,' Thenmozhi told him. 'Chithi pours at dawn, when the air is cool. I will show you everything.'

Next morning she led him to a table at the back of the workshop. On it stood a dancer as tall as Thenmozhi's forearm, the colour of honey. Kabir touched her with one finger. She was smooth and a little soft.
'Wax,' said Thenmozhi. 'Beeswax mixed with tree resin and a little oil. Chithi shaped her with warm fingers. When the wax is warm it bends. When it cools it holds.'
'But a wax dancer will melt in the sun,' said Kabir.
'That is the plan,' said Thenmozhi. 'She has to melt.'

She showed him the next table. Here a second figure was hidden inside a thick coat of clay. 'Fine clay from the bed of the Kaveri goes on first,' she said. 'It is pressed into every line of the wax. Then comes thicker clay. We leave a hole at the bottom. Then it dries for days.'
Out in the yard, Valli Chithi was setting a dry clay mould beside a fire pit, with the hole facing down. 'Both of you stay behind the rope,' she said. They stayed behind the rope.
Soon a thin golden stream ran out of the hole into a pan. Kabir stared. 'The dancer is running away!'

'The wax is,' said Thenmozhi. 'Wax melts at about sixty degrees. That is not much hotter than a tumbler of tea. Clay does not care about sixty degrees. So now there is a dancer-shaped hole inside the clay. Nothing but air, in the shape of her.'
Kabir thought about a hole that had fingers and a nose. It made his head feel strange.
Across the yard a clay pot sat deep in glowing charcoal. A worker named Selvi was feeding it pieces of metal. In went a cracked lamp, a handful of old bells and some bars of copper.
'That is my grandmother's broken lamp,' said Thenmozhi. 'Chithi asked her first.'
'How hot is it in there?' asked Kabir.
'More than a thousand degrees. Copper will not melt below that.'

Kabir whistled. In Delhi in January, he said, the coconut oil in their kitchen turned white and hard in the bottle. His father stood the bottle in a mug of warm water every morning. Twenty-four degrees was enough to melt that.
'And ice needs only zero,' said Thenmozhi. 'Everything has its own number.'

Valli Chithi and Selvi lifted the pot with long tongs. The metal inside was bright orange and moved like thick buttermilk. They tipped it into the hole of the mould. It went in with a soft glugging sound. Then there was nothing to see. The mould just sat there.
'Now we wait for it to freeze,' said Thenmozhi.
Kabir laughed. 'Freeze? It is hotter than anything I have ever seen.'

'Chithi calls it freezing, and she is right,' said Thenmozhi. 'Listen. This bronze turns solid a little below a thousand degrees. So when it has cooled to nine hundred, it is a solid. It is still glowing red. It could still set wood on fire. But it is frozen.'
Kabir was quiet for a while. 'So for bronze, nine hundred degrees is cold.'
'Cold enough to freeze,' said Thenmozhi. 'And for ice, your hand is terribly hot. And wax is somewhere in between.'
'Then what is hot?'
'I asked Chithi that when I was seven,' said Thenmozhi. 'She said, hot for whom?'
They came back the next morning, when the mould was cool enough to hold. Valli Chithi gave Thenmozhi the small hammer. 'You open it.'
Thenmozhi tapped. The clay cracked and fell away in pieces. Inside, dark and rough and dusted with ash, stood the dancer. Every finger was there. The line of her eyebrow was there.
Kabir looked at her for a long time. 'Yesterday she was wax,' he said slowly. 'Then she was a hole. Now she is bronze. And the bronze was a lamp and some bells.'
'And the wax is in the pan,' said Thenmozhi. 'It set again overnight. Next week Chithi will shape that same wax into something new.'
'So where is the dancer?' asked Kabir. 'Is she the bronze? The bronze was here before her. Is she the shape? The shape was in wax first, and then in nothing at all.'

Thenmozhi began to answer, and stopped. She had opened forty moulds and had never once asked that. She looked at the pan of pale wax. She looked at her grandmother's lamp, which now had fingers and an eyebrow.
'Ask me again tomorrow,' she said. 'I need to think.'
story.epiphany: Kabir saw that bronze 'freezes' while it is still red-hot, so hot and cold are not fixed things. They depend on whose melting point you ask about. He also saw the same shape pass from wax to an empty space to bronze, while the bronze itself had been a lamp the day before.
ask: Thenmozhi said bronze at nine hundred degrees is frozen. Do you agree that this is freezing? Why?
Where do you think the dancer is: in the bronze, in the shape, or somewhere else?
The wax will be melted and shaped again, and so might the bronze one day. What stays the same through all the melting?
