experiments.title: The Salt Test: which ice melts most, and which bowl gets coldest?
experiments.context: In this experiment you sprinkle salt on one bowl of ice, sugar on another and nothing on a third. You measure the meltwater and feel the bowls, to find out what salt really does to ice.
experiments.question: If you sprinkle salt on ice cubes, do they melt faster or slower than plain ice? Does sugar do the same? And which bowl ends up the coldest?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess two things. Which bowl will have the most meltwater after 15 minutes: plain, salt or sugar? Which bowl will feel the coldest on the outside? Give a reason for each guess.
experiments.fair_test: All three bowls are the same size and made of the same steel. Each gets four ice cubes from the same tray, taken out at the same moment. The bowls stand side by side, away from the window and the fan, for the same 15 minutes. Only one thing changes: what is sprinkled on the ice. Each bowl has four cubes, so one odd cube matters less. If you have a second tray of ice, do the whole test twice, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: How the outside felt at 5 and 10 minutes

materials.item: ice cubes of the same size, from one tray (make them the day before)
small steel bowls (katoris) of the same size
table salt, one level teaspoon
sugar, one level teaspoon
a measuring teaspoon and one more spoon
an empty tumbler to measure meltwater into
a clock or timer, three paper labels, a pencil and a cloth

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write three lines: what I think, what I saw, and why I think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results in a room at 29 degrees (yours will be different)

setup.art: Three small steel bowls in a row on a kitchen counter with paper labels: Plain, Sugar, Salt. Each holds four ice cubes.
setup.caption: 1. Label three bowls. Put four ice cubes in each.

setup.art: A hand sprinkling a level teaspoon of salt over the ice in the bowl labelled Salt, with a spoon of sugar waiting beside the Sugar bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Sprinkle one level teaspoon of sugar on one bowl and one of salt on another. Leave the third plain.

setup.art: A child touching the outside of each bowl with one fingertip, with a clock showing 5 minutes gone.
setup.caption: 3. At 5 and 10 minutes, touch the outside of each bowl for two seconds.

setup.art: A spoon holding back ice cubes while meltwater is poured from a bowl into a tumbler, and a teaspoon measuring the water back out.
setup.caption: 4. At 15 minutes, hold the ice back and pour off the meltwater. Count it in teaspoons.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Salt Test. You guess before you try.
flow.do: Show the three bowls, the salt and the sugar. Ask for both guesses and a reason for each. Write them down.
flow.say: One bowl gets salt, one gets sugar and one gets nothing. Which will melt the most in 15 minutes? Which bowl will feel the coldest? Tell me why you think so.
flow.kid: Look at the three bowls. Guess which ice will melt the most. Guess which bowl will be coldest. Say why.

ask.q: Which bowl will have the most meltwater, and why?
good: Salt, because I have heard salt melts ice.
Plain, because salt and sugar are not warm.
All the same, because the room is the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children say the bowl that melts most must be the warmest. Let the test answer that.

flow.do: 1. Label the bowls Plain, Sugar and Salt. 2. Put four ice cubes in each. 3. Sprinkle one level teaspoon of sugar over the Sugar bowl. 4. Sprinkle one level teaspoon of salt over the Salt bowl. 5. Start the clock.
flow.say: Each bowl gets four cubes from the same tray. Level the teaspoon with your finger, so that the sugar and the salt are the same amount. Start the clock now.
flow.kid: Put four ice cubes in each bowl. Sprinkle one level spoon of sugar on one. Sprinkle one level spoon of salt on another. Start the clock.
flow.parent: Work quickly so that all the ice starts at the same time. Keep the bowls a hand apart and away from sunlight and the fan.

flow.do: 1. Wait and watch. 2. At 5 minutes and at 10 minutes, touch the outside of each bowl with one fingertip for two seconds. 3. Write how each one feels. 4. Look for dew or frost on the outside of the bowls.
flow.say: While we wait, look closely. Touch the outside of each bowl for two seconds. Which is the coldest? Is anything forming on the outside of the bowls?
flow.kid: Watch the ice. At 5 and 10 minutes, touch each bowl outside for two seconds. Write which one is coldest.

ask.q: What do you notice about the Salt bowl?
good: The ice looks wet and has holes in it.
It is the coldest to touch.
There is frost or a lot of dew on the outside.

flow.parent: On a damp day the Salt bowl may grow white frost on the outside. That shows it is below 0 degrees. Touch for two seconds only, because the Salt bowl is very cold.

flow.do: 1. At 15 minutes, take the Plain bowl. 2. Hold the ice back with a spoon and pour the meltwater into the tumbler. 3. Spoon the water back into the sink, counting level teaspoons. 4. Write the number. 5. Do the same for Sugar and then Salt.
flow.say: Now we measure. Hold the ice back and pour off only the water. Count the teaspoons. Write each number in the table before you do the next bowl.
flow.kid: Pour the water from one bowl into the tumbler. Keep the ice back. Count the water in teaspoons and write it down.
flow.parent: If the room is cool and there is less than one teaspoon in the Plain bowl, wait 10 minutes more for all three bowls. The salty water is not for drinking. Pour it down the sink.

flow.do: Ask your child to write three lines: what I think, what I saw, why. Then ask what the test cannot tell us.
flow.say: Write what you think salt does to ice. Write what you saw that shows it. Then say why you think it happened. Was anything a surprise?
flow.kid: Write three lines. What do I think? What did I see? Why did it happen?

ask.q: The salted ice melted most but its bowl was coldest. How can both be true?
good: Melting takes heat, and it took the heat from the bowl.
The salt did not warm the ice. Something else made it melt.

ask.q: What can this test not tell us?
good: It cannot show the particles.
It does not tell us if more salt would melt more.
It does not tell us what happens in a freezer.

flow.think: Would salt melt ice inside a freezer at minus 18 degrees? How could you find out?

check.q: Why did the Salt bowl get colder?
options: Melting takes in heat from the bowl and the ice
The salt blocked the warm air
check.why: Melting always takes in heat. Nobody was heating the bowl, so the heat came from the ice, the salty water and the bowl, and they got colder. Salt from the shelf is at room temperature. It is not cold.

flow.parent: Read the card 'Why salt melts ice, and makes it colder' only after your child has written the three lines.

experiments.title: The Flat Line: does melting ice get warmer?
experiments.context: In this experiment you read a thermometer every three minutes in a tumbler of ice and water, and in a tumbler of cold water with no ice. You find out where the room's heat goes. It needs a kitchen thermometer.
experiments.question: A tumbler of ice and water and a tumbler of cold water stand in the same warm room. Do they warm up in the same way? What happens to the temperature when salt goes into the icy one?
experiments.predict: Guess what each thermometer reading will be after 15 minutes. Will the icy tumbler warm up, stay the same or get colder? Then guess what two spoons of salt will do to its temperature. Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Both tumblers are the same size and material and hold the same amount in total. They stand side by side. You stir each one for ten seconds before every reading, and read at the same times. Only one thing is different: one has ice in it. The salt goes in only at the end, as a second test.

materials.item: a digital kitchen thermometer with a metal probe, which can read below 0 degrees
plastic or steel tumblers of the same size
ice cubes
cold water from the fridge, about one and a half tumblers
table salt, two level teaspoons
a spoon, a clock, a pencil and paper

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then mark your readings as dots on squared paper, minutes along the bottom and degrees up the side, and join the dots for each tumbler.

example_chart.title: Made-up example readings in a room at 29 degrees (yours will be different)

setup.art: Two identical steel tumblers side by side: A with six ice cubes and water to half way, B with cold water to the same height and no ice.
setup.caption: 1. Tumbler A gets six ice cubes and cold water up to half way. Tumbler B gets cold water to the same height.

setup.art: A child stirring tumbler A with a spoon and holding a digital probe thermometer in the water, with the reading 0 on the screen.
setup.caption: 2. Stir for ten seconds, then read the thermometer. Do this for each tumbler every three minutes.

setup.art: A teaspoon of salt being tipped into tumbler A, with the thermometer screen showing a minus sign.
setup.caption: 3. After 15 minutes, stir two teaspoons of salt into tumbler A and read again.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Flat Line test. You guess before you measure.
flow.do: Show the two tumblers and the thermometer. Ask for a guess for each tumbler after 15 minutes, with a reason. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: Both tumblers will sit in this warm room. Heat will flow into both. What will each thermometer reading be after 15 minutes? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess the temperature of each tumbler after 15 minutes. Say why you think so.
flow.parent: Most children expect both to warm up, the icy one a little less. Do not correct the guess.

flow.do: 1. Put six ice cubes in tumbler A. 2. Add cold water up to half way. 3. Fill tumbler B to the same height with cold water. 4. Stir each for ten seconds. 5. Read the temperature of each and write it at 0 minutes.
flow.say: Stir first, then read. Hold the tip of the probe in the middle of the water, away from the wall of the tumbler. Wait until the number stops changing.
flow.kid: Fill both tumblers. Stir each one. Put the probe in the middle and read the number. Write it down.
flow.parent: The probe has a pointed tip, so hand it over handle first and wipe it between tumblers.

flow.do: 1. Every three minutes, stir each tumbler for ten seconds and read the temperature. 2. Write each reading in the table. 3. Go on until 15 minutes.
flow.say: Read both tumblers every three minutes. Write the number straight away. Look at how much ice is left each time.
flow.kid: Every three minutes, stir and read both tumblers. Write the numbers. Look at how much ice is left.

ask.q: What is happening to the number in A, and to the ice in A?
good: The number stays at about 0.
The ice is getting smaller.
B is warming up but A is not.

flow.parent: Tumbler A should stay within one degree of 0 while ice is left. If it reads 2 or 3, stir for longer, because the water at the bottom warms first.

flow.do: 1. Add two level teaspoons of salt to tumbler A. 2. Stir for one minute. 3. Read the temperature. 4. Write it down.
flow.say: Now the salt. Guess the number first. Then stir for a full minute and read. Look for a minus sign.
flow.kid: Guess first. Then stir two spoons of salt into tumbler A. Read the number. Is there a minus sign?
flow.parent: With ice still in the tumbler, the reading usually falls to between minus 2 and minus 6. If all the ice has gone, add three fresh cubes before the salt.

flow.do: Ask your child to write three lines: what I think, what I saw, why. Pour the salty water down the sink.
flow.say: Heat went into both tumblers. Only one got warmer. Write where you think the heat in tumbler A went.
flow.kid: Write three lines. What do I think? What did I see? Where did the heat go?

ask.q: Heat flowed into A the whole time. Why did the number not go up?
good: The heat was used to melt the ice.
The ice got smaller instead of the water getting warmer.

flow.think: The salt made the number go below 0. Where did that heat go?

check.q: When will tumbler A start to warm up?
options: When the last ice has melted
check.why: While any ice is left, the heat coming in is used for melting. Only when the ice has gone can the heat make the water warmer. It depends on the ice, not on the clock or the room.

activities.title: Ghee There and Back
activities.context: In this activity you melt a little ghee and coconut oil over warm water and set them again over ice water. You watch closely how each one changes. It opens the lesson.

materials.item: ghee, half a teaspoon
coconut oil, half a teaspoon
small steel bowls (katoris) that can float
wider bowls, one for warm water and one for cold water
ice cubes
warm water, as warm as a bath, two tumblers

activities.safety: A grown-up pours the warm water. It should be no warmer than a bath, so that a hand can rest in it.
activities.record: Draw the ghee and the coconut oil three times: at the start, over warm water and over cold water. Write one word under each drawing.

setup.art: Two small steel bowls, one with a dab of grainy white ghee and one with a dab of coconut oil, floating in a wider bowl of warm water.
setup.caption: 1. Float the two small bowls on warm water. Watch the ghee and the oil.

setup.art: The same two small bowls now floating in a wider bowl of water with four ice cubes, the oil turning white from the edge.
setup.caption: 2. Move the small bowls to the ice water. Watch them again.

flow.context: This is the first step of Ghee There and Back. You look and guess.
flow.do: Put half a teaspoon of ghee in one small bowl and half a teaspoon of coconut oil in the other. Ask your child to describe each one and guess what warm water will do.
flow.say: Look at the ghee and the oil. Is each one a solid or a liquid right now? Which will change first over warm water? Why?
flow.kid: Look at the ghee and the oil. Is each one solid or liquid now? Guess which will change first.
flow.parent: If your kitchen is warm and both are already liquid, do the ice water step first and the warm water step second.

flow.do: 1. Pour warm water into one wide bowl. 2. Float both small bowls on it. 3. Watch for three minutes. 4. Ask where the melting starts.
flow.say: Watch the edge of the ghee. Does it melt all at once or bit by bit? Which one turned clear first?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to pour the warm water. Float the two bowls. Watch where the melting starts.

ask.q: Did the ghee melt all at once?
good: No, the grains stayed for a while in the clear part.
It melted from the edge that touched the bowl.

flow.do: 1. Put cold water and four ice cubes in the other wide bowl. 2. Move the two small bowls onto it. 3. Watch for three minutes. 4. Tilt each small bowl to see if it still flows.
flow.say: Now the heat goes the other way, out of the oil and into the cold water. Watch the colour. Tilt the bowl gently. Does it still flow?
flow.kid: Float the two bowls on the ice water. Watch the colour change. Tilt each bowl. Does it flow?

ask.q: What did you see as it set?
good: The oil turned white from the edge.
The ghee went cloudy and thick.
It stopped flowing.

flow.do: Ask what was the same and what was different between the start and the end. Scrape the ghee and oil back for cooking.
flow.say: Is it the same ghee as before? What changed and what did not? What decided whether it was solid or liquid?
flow.kid: Is it the same ghee as at the start? What changed? What made it change?
flow.think: The ghee got grainy and the oil did not. What might be different inside them?

activities.title: Dip or Bump? What happens to the size
activities.context: In this activity you mark the level of water and of melted coconut oil, let both turn solid overnight and compare. You find out which one grows and which one shrinks.

materials.item: plastic tumblers of the same size (not glass)
water, half a tumbler
coconut oil, half a tumbler (it goes back in the bottle afterwards)
a marker pen or two rubber bands
space in the freezer and in the fridge

schedule.what: Mark the levels, guess, and put the water in the freezer and the oil in the fridge.
Take both out, compare each surface with its line, and talk about why.

activities.safety: If the coconut oil is solid, a grown-up stands the bottle in warm water first. Use plastic tumblers, because glass can crack in a freezer.
activities.record: Draw each tumbler from the side on both days. Show the line and the surface.

setup.art: Two plastic tumblers, one half full of water and one half full of clear coconut oil, each with a marker line exactly at the surface.
setup.caption: 1. Half fill one tumbler with water and one with liquid coconut oil. Mark each level.

setup.art: The same tumblers next day: the ice bulging above its line with a bump in the middle, the white set oil below its line with a dip in the middle.
setup.caption: 2. Next day, compare each surface with its line.

flow.context: This is the first step of Dip or Bump. You set up two tumblers and mark them.
flow.do: 1. If the oil is solid, stand its bottle in warm water until it is clear. 2. Half fill one tumbler with water and the other with oil. 3. Mark each level with the pen or a rubber band.
flow.say: Both are liquids now. Mark the line exactly at the surface. Bend down so that your eyes are level with it.
flow.kid: Half fill one tumbler with water and one with oil. Mark each level exactly. A grown-up warms the oil if needed.

flow.do: Ask for a guess with a reason. Then put the water in the freezer and the oil in the fridge. Leave both until tomorrow.
flow.say: When each one turns solid, will its surface be above the line, below it or on it? Will both do the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess where each surface will be tomorrow. Say why. Put the water in the freezer and the oil in the fridge.

flow.do: 1. Take both tumblers out. 2. Look at each surface from the side. 3. Compare it with its line. 4. Look at the shape of each top.
flow.say: Look from the side. Where is the ice compared with its line? Where is the oil? What shape is the top of each one?
flow.kid: Take both out. Look from the side. Is each surface above or below its line? What shape is the top?

good: The ice went above the line and has a bump.
The oil went a little below the line and has a dip or a crack.

flow.parent: The ice rises clearly, by about one tenth of its height. The oil sinks only a little. Look for a dip, a crack or a gap at the wall.

flow.do: Talk about why. Then stand the oil tumbler in warm water and pour the oil back into its bottle. Let the ice melt and use the water for a potted plant.
flow.say: One grew and one shrank. Both are the same amount of substance as yesterday. So what must have changed inside?
flow.kid: One grew and one shrank. Nothing was added. What changed inside? A grown-up warms the oil to pour it back.
flow.think: Ice floats on water. Would a lump of solid coconut oil float or sink in melted coconut oil?

activities.title: Flash Freeze: can you catch water below zero?
activities.context: In this activity you cool sealed bottles of clean water in the freezer and try to catch them while they are below 0 degrees and still liquid. It does not work every time, and that is part of what it teaches.

materials.item: small sealed plastic bottles of packaged drinking water, 250 to 500 millilitres, unopened
space in the freezer where the bottles can lie flat and not touch
a steel bowl and one ice cube
a clock or timer

activities.record: Write the time each bottle spent in the freezer and what happened: still liquid, flash froze, or already solid.

setup.art: Three small sealed plastic water bottles lying flat on a freezer shelf, not touching each other.
setup.caption: 1. Lay three sealed bottles flat in the freezer. Do not move them.

setup.art: A hand knocking the base of a bottle on a table, with white ice racing down through the clear water.
setup.caption: 2. Lift one out gently. If the water is still liquid, knock the bottle once on the table.

setup.art: Very cold water being poured slowly from a bottle onto one ice cube in a steel bowl, building a small tower of slush.
setup.caption: 3. Or pour the cold water slowly onto an ice cube and watch a slush tower grow.

flow.context: This is the first step of Flash Freeze. You set the bottles in the freezer and note the time.
flow.do: 1. Lay the three sealed bottles flat in the freezer, not touching. 2. Write down the time. 3. Ask what your child expects to find in two hours.
flow.say: The freezer is at about minus 18 degrees. Water freezes at 0. What will be in these bottles in two hours? Why?
flow.kid: Lay three bottles flat in the freezer. Write the time. Guess what they will look like in two hours.
flow.wait: Leave small bottles for about 1 hour 30 minutes and half-litre bottles for about 2 hours. Do not open the freezer in between.
flow.parent: Freezers differ. The three bottles let you try three times: take one out, and leave the others for 15 minutes more if needed.

flow.do: 1. Lift one bottle out very gently. 2. Look. 3. If the water is liquid, knock the bottle firmly once on the table. 4. Watch the water.
flow.say: Carry it like a sleeping baby. Is it liquid? Then knock it once and watch closely.
flow.kid: Lift one bottle out gently. Is the water still liquid? Knock the bottle once on the table. Watch.

good: White ice spread through the bottle in a few seconds.
It turned to slush, not a hard block.
Nothing happened, so it was not cold enough yet.

flow.parent: If nothing happens, the water is not yet below 0. Put the other bottles back for 15 minutes. If a bottle is already solid, it froze by itself, so take the next one out sooner next time. Expect about one success in three tries.

flow.do: With another liquid bottle, open it gently and pour slowly onto one ice cube in the bowl. Then talk about what started the freezing.
flow.say: The water was colder than 0 and still liquid. What was it waiting for? What did the knock or the ice cube give it?
flow.kid: Pour the cold water slowly onto an ice cube. Watch what grows. What was the water waiting for?
flow.think: The slush is not a hard block. Why did only part of the water freeze?

activities.title: The Kulfi Maker's Trick: freeze sweet milk without a freezer
activities.context: In this activity you stand one tumbler of sweet milk in plain ice and one in ice with salt, and stir both. You find out why kulfi sellers add salt to their ice, and you eat the result.

materials.item: ice cubes (two trays)
salt, four tablespoons (rock salt or table salt)
small steel tumblers
bowls deep enough for the ice to reach half way up a tumbler
milk, six tablespoons, and sugar, one teaspoon
teaspoons for stirring, and a cloth

activities.safety: Ice mixed with salt is far colder than plain ice and can hurt skin. A grown-up mixes it. Nobody holds the salted ice in a bare hand. Keep the salty water out of the milk.
activities.record: Write what the milk in each tumbler was like after 12 minutes: liquid, slushy or frozen.

setup.art: Two bowls of ice cubes, one labelled Plain and one labelled Salt with salt sprinkled over the ice, each with a small steel tumbler of milk standing in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Stand a tumbler of sweet milk in each bowl of ice. One bowl has salt on the ice.

setup.art: A child stirring the milk in the tumbler in the Salt bowl and scraping frozen milk off the inside wall with a teaspoon.
setup.caption: 2. Stir both milks and scrape the walls of the tumblers for 12 minutes.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Kulfi Maker's Trick. You guess before you try.
flow.do: Stir the sugar into the milk. Put three tablespoons of sweet milk in each steel tumbler. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: Plain ice is at 0 degrees. Sweet milk freezes a little below 0. Can plain ice freeze this milk? Can ice with salt? Why?
flow.kid: Put three spoons of sweet milk in each tumbler. Guess which ice can freeze the milk. Say why.

flow.do: 1. Put 12 ice cubes in each bowl. 2. Add two tablespoons of water to each. 3. Mix four tablespoons of salt into one bowl of ice with a spoon. 4. Stand a tumbler of milk in the middle of each bowl.
flow.say: I will mix the salt in with a spoon. Do not touch the salted ice with your hands. It is much colder than plain ice.
flow.kid: A grown-up mixes salt into one bowl of ice. Do not touch that ice. Stand a tumbler in each bowl.
flow.parent: Push the ice up around each tumbler so that it reaches at least half way up the side.

flow.do: 1. Stir each milk with its own spoon. 2. Scrape the inside wall of each tumbler every minute. 3. Compare the two milks every three minutes.
flow.say: Scrape the wall of the tumbler, because that is where the cold comes in. What do you feel on the spoon in each one?
flow.kid: Stir both milks. Scrape the inside wall each minute. Look at what is forming on the wall.

ask.q: What is different between the two tumblers?
good: The milk in the salt bowl is freezing on the wall.
The milk in plain ice is only cold.
The salt bowl has more water in it.

flow.parent: If the milk in the Salt bowl is still fully liquid after 12 minutes, mix in two more tablespoons of salt and go on for 5 minutes.

flow.do: Lift the tumblers out and wipe the outsides. Eat the frozen milk. Talk about what the salt did. Pour the salty water down the sink.
flow.say: Both bowls had the same ice. Only one froze the milk. What did the salt do to the ice? Where did the milk's heat go?
flow.kid: Wipe the tumblers and taste both milks. Only one froze. What did the salt do to the ice?
flow.think: A kulfi seller keeps adding salt and ice all afternoon. Why does the pot need more of both?

games.title: The Melting Point Ladder
games.context: In this card game you build a ladder of substances from the coldest melting point to the hottest. You must reason about where each new card goes before you turn it over.

setup.art: A row of cards on a table with their number sides up, from minus 219 on the left to 1,538 on the right, and a pile of unplayed cards beside it.
setup.caption: 1. The ladder is a row of cards with the number side up, coldest on the left.

setup.art: A child holding a card that says Candle wax above a gap between the cards for coconut oil and tin, about to place it.
setup.caption: 2. Read the front of the top card, choose its place in the ladder, then turn it over to check.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a substance on the front, and its melting point in degrees Celsius on the back

items.b: About minus 272, and only when squeezed hard. In the open it stays liquid down to the coldest temperature there is.

items.f: Oxygen, the part of air we breathe in
Mercury, the silver liquid in old thermometers

items.b: About minus 2. The salt lowers it.
About 30. It melts in a warm hand.
From about 28 to about 40. Ghee is a mixture, so it melts bit by bit. Any place between coconut oil and candle wax is right.

items.f: Lead, the metal in car batteries
Zinc, the coating on iron buckets

items.b: No exact melting point. It softens from about 600 to 1,000. Any place between zinc and gold is right. Say why it has no single place.

items.f: Tungsten, the wire in old light bulbs

rules: Shuffle the 24 cards and make a pile with the fronts up. Nobody looks at the backs.
Take the top card, read it aloud and turn it over. Put it in the middle of the table with the number side up. This is the start of the ladder.

Take turns. On your turn, read the front of the top card aloud. Say where it goes in the ladder: to the left of all the cards (colder), to the right of all (hotter), or between two cards. Give a reason.
Turn the card over. If your place was right, you score 1 point. Right or wrong, put the card in its correct place, number side up.
Two cards, ghee and window glass, have a stretch of temperatures. Their backs say which places count as right.
Keep the score with tally marks on paper. The ladder gets longer, so each turn is harder than the last.
The game ends when the pile is empty. The player with the most points wins. A tie is a shared win.
Playing alone, try to score at least 16 points out of 23.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Melting Point Ladder. You set up the pile and the first card.
flow.do: Shuffle the cards. Make a pile with the fronts up. Turn the first card over to start the ladder. Read the rules together.
flow.say: Each card names a substance. Its melting point is on the back. We will build a row from the coldest melting point to the hottest.
flow.kid: Shuffle the cards and make a pile, fronts up. Turn over the first card to start the ladder.

flow.do: Play in turns until the pile is empty. Ask for a reason before each card is turned over. Keep the score with tally marks.
flow.say: Before you turn it over, tell me your reason. Have you seen this substance melt? Is it liquid or solid in our kitchen?
flow.kid: Read the top card. Choose its place and say why. Then turn it over and check.

ask.q: How did you decide where it goes?
good: It is a liquid in our room, so it melts below room temperature.
It is part of the air, so it must melt far below 0.
It is used for cooking pans, so it melts very high.

flow.parent: A good clue is the state at room temperature. Something that is part of the air melts far below 0. A liquid melts below about 25. A solid melts above that.

flow.do: Look at the finished ladder together. Ask which card surprised your child most, and what the two stretch cards have in common.
flow.say: Look at the whole ladder. Where is the biggest jump? Which card surprised you? Why do ghee and glass not have one number?
flow.kid: Look at the whole ladder. Which card surprised you most? Why do ghee and glass have no single number?
flow.think: Where on this ladder would you put yourself? Is there one answer?

projects.title: Cast It Twice: one substance, two shapes
projects.context: In this project you make a hollow mould, pour in a melted substance and let it solidify, the way bronze casters in Swamimalai do. Then you melt the casting and cast the same substance into a new shape.

materials.item: stiff atta dough kneaded with a few drops of oil, or modelling clay, in balls the size of a lemon
small hard objects to press in, such as a shell, a key, a big button or a small toy
coconut oil, four tablespoons (in a hot place use ghee)
water, four tablespoons
a steel plate, a spoon, and space in the fridge and the freezer
a small steel bowl and a wider bowl of warm water, for melting

schedule.what: Make two moulds from one object. Pour water into one and melted oil into the other. Freeze and chill them overnight.
Lift out both castings and compare them. Melt the oil casting and pour the same oil into a mould of a different shape.
Lift out the second casting. Draw both shapes and write what stayed the same.

projects.safety: A grown-up pours the warm water for melting the oil. It should be no warmer than a bath.
projects.record: Keep a page with drawings of the object, the mould, the ice casting, the first oil casting and the second oil casting. Write under them what stayed the same and what changed.

setup.art: A shell being pressed half way into a flattened ball of dough on a steel plate, and a second dough mould beside it with a clear shell-shaped hollow.
setup.caption: 1. Press the object half way into the dough and lift it out. You now have a hollow in its shape.

setup.art: A spoon pouring clear melted coconut oil into a shell-shaped hollow in dough, with a second mould already filled with water.
setup.caption: 2. Fill one hollow with water and one with melted oil. Freeze the water and chill the oil.

setup.art: A white shell-shaped casting of set coconut oil next to a shell-shaped piece of ice and the real shell.
setup.caption: 3. Next day, lift out the castings and compare them with the object.

flow.context: This is the first step of Cast It Twice. You make the moulds.
flow.do: 1. Flatten two balls of dough on the steel plate, two fingers thick. 2. Press the same object half way into each. 3. Lift it straight out. 4. Check that each hollow has a clean edge.
flow.say: The hollow is the shape of the object, but there is nothing in it. Bronze casters call this the mould. We will fill it with a liquid.
flow.kid: Flatten the dough. Press the object in half way. Lift it straight out. Look at the hollow.

flow.do: 1. Melt the coconut oil in the small bowl floating on warm water. 2. Spoon water into one hollow up to the edge. 3. Spoon melted oil into the other. 4. Put the water mould in the freezer and the oil mould in the fridge.
flow.say: Which casting will copy the fine lines better, the ice or the oil? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A grown-up melts the oil. Fill one hollow with water and one with oil. Guess which will copy the shape better.

flow.do: 1. Peel the dough away from each casting. 2. Compare both with the object. 3. Make a new mould from a different object. 4. Melt the oil casting over warm water and pour it into the new mould. 5. Chill it overnight.
flow.say: Look at the lines and edges. Which copied better? Now we melt this shape and give the same oil a new one.
flow.kid: Peel off the dough. Compare the two castings. Then a grown-up melts the oil one. Pour it into a new mould.

ask.q: When the oil casting melted, where did the shape go?
good: The oil is still here but the shape is gone.
The shape was in the mould, not in the oil.

flow.wait: Leave the new mould in the fridge overnight.
flow.parent: The ice casting often has a bump on top and may crack the dough a little, because water grows as it freezes. The oil casting has a small dip.

flow.do: Lift out the second casting. Ask your child to draw every stage and to write what stayed the same. Keep the oil for a lamp or for oiling a hinge, not for cooking.
flow.say: It was one shape yesterday and another today. Is it the same oil? What stayed the same, and what did not?
flow.kid: Lift out the new casting. Draw every stage. Write what stayed the same and what changed.
flow.think: A caster in Swamimalai melts an old lamp to make a new figure. Is the figure the lamp?

challenges.title: Free the Coin: the fastest rescue from ice
challenges.context: In this challenge a coin is frozen inside a block of ice. You have to get it out as fast as you can, using what you know about how heat gets into ice. There is more than one good way.
challenges.problem: A coin is frozen in the middle of a block of ice. Get the coin out as fast as you can.
constraints: No warm or heated water, and no heater, iron or hair dryer.
No hitting, cutting or breaking the ice.
You may use only things from the list.
Each method gets its own ice block, and you time each one.
materials: 3 ice blocks, each with a coin inside (the day before, put a coin in each of 3 small steel bowls, half fill with water and freeze)
a tumbler of tap water and a wide bowl
a steel plate, a steel spoon, a cloth and a hand fan or a sheet of card
general: Pour tap water slowly over the block. Tap water is 20 degrees or more above the melting point of ice, and moving water keeps bringing fresh heat.
Rub salt onto the block. The salt lowers the melting point at the surface, so the ice melts even while it is very cold.
Hold the block in your hands. Your skin is at about 34 degrees.
creative: Lay the block on a steel plate and press it down. Metal carries heat from the room into the ice far faster than air does.
Fan the block hard. Moving air brings more of the room's heat to the ice than still air.
Sprinkle salt in one line across the block, so that it melts a groove straight down to the coin.
challenges.your_turn: Now think of a method that is not on either list, or join two methods together. Guess its time first. There is no single best answer: the fastest way in a hot kitchen in Chennai may not be the fastest in a cold one in Shimla.

setup.art: Three small steel bowls half full of water, each with a coin at the bottom, on a freezer shelf.
setup.caption: 1. The day before: freeze a coin in water in each of three small bowls.

setup.art: Three ice blocks with coins inside on a counter: one under a thin stream of tap water, one rubbed with salt, one sitting on a steel plate.
setup.caption: 2. Try a different method on each block and time each one.

flow.context: This is the first step of Free the Coin. You plan before you touch the ice.
flow.do: Read the problem and the rules aloud. Look at the things on the list. Ask your child to choose three methods and guess which will be fastest.
flow.say: The coin can come out only when the ice around it melts. Melting needs heat. Where could the heat come from? Choose three ways and guess the fastest.
flow.kid: Read the rules. Think about where heat can come from. Choose three ways. Guess which is fastest.

ask.q: Where can the heat for melting come from?
good: From tap water.
From my hands.
From the air in the room.
From a metal plate.

flow.parent: Dip each bowl in tap water for a few seconds to loosen the block before you start.

flow.do: 1. Start the first method and the clock together. 2. Stop the clock when the coin comes free. 3. Write the time. 4. Do the same for the other two methods.
flow.say: Start the clock as you begin. Stop it the moment the coin is free. Write the time before you start the next one.
flow.kid: Start the clock and the method together. Stop when the coin is free. Write the time. Then try the next way.
flow.parent: If you have the hands, run all three at once to save time. Stop any method at 10 minutes and write 'more than 10'.

flow.do: Compare the three times. Ask why the fastest was fastest. Then read the two lists of solutions together.
flow.say: Which was fastest? What brought heat to the ice quickest? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Compare the three times. Why was the fastest one fastest?

ask.q: Why does running water beat still air?
good: Water carries more heat than air.
It keeps moving, so fresh warm water keeps coming.

flow.do: Ask for one new method or a mix of two. Let your child guess its time. Try it another day with a fresh block.
flow.say: Now invent your own way, or join two together. Guess its time first. We will freeze another coin tonight.
flow.kid: Invent your own way, or join two ways. Guess its time. Freeze another coin for tomorrow.
flow.think: Salt gave the ice no heat at all. So where did the heat come from when the salt melted the ice?

worksheets.title: Melting and solidifying: the main ideas

items.p: Butter on a hot dosa turns runny. Which change is this?
items.why: Melting. One substance, butter, turns into its own liquid because of heat. Dissolving would need a second substance, a liquid for the butter to spread into.

items.p: Coconut oil melts at about 24 degrees. The kitchen is at 19 degrees. What is the oil?
items.why: A solid. 19 is below 24, so the oil is colder than its melting point. If you chose liquid, compare the two numbers again: below the melting point means solid.

items.p: Melted candle wax drips on a table and turns hard. Where did its heat go?
opts: Into the table and the air
It was used up and is gone
items.why: A liquid gives out heat as it solidifies, and the heat goes into whatever it touches. Heat is not used up. You can feel the table warm under a fresh wax drop.

items.p: Iron melts at 1,538 degrees and wax at about 60. Which has stronger pulls between its particles?
items.why: Iron. Stronger pulls hold the particles in place more firmly, so the solid must be much hotter before they break free.

items.p: Sugar stirred into cold water seems to vanish. Which change is this?
items.why: Dissolving. There are two substances, and the water is far colder than the temperature at which sugar turns liquid. If you chose melting, count the substances.

items.p: True or false: water is the only substance that can freeze.
items.why: False. Freezing means a liquid turning solid. Melted wax, ghee, gold and iron all freeze, each at its own temperature.

items.p: True or false: ice and liquid water are made of the same particles.
items.why: True. The particles are the same. In ice they are held in place, and in water they slide past each other.

items.p: The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid is its ____ ____.
items.why: Each pure substance has its own melting point. For ice it is 0 degrees Celsius.

items.p: A change that can be undone, giving the same substance back, is a ____ change.
items.why: Melting is undone by solidifying, so both are reversible changes.

items.p: Match each solid to its melting point in degrees Celsius.
items.why: Ice melts in a cool room, coconut oil on a warm day, wax near a flame and iron only in a furnace.

items.p: Sort each change: is it melting or dissolving?
items.why: Melting needs one substance and heat. Dissolving needs a solid and a different liquid for it to spread into.

items.p: Put in order what the particles do as ice from the freezer warms up and melts.
items: Particles at the surface break out of their places
The particles shake a little on the spot
The particles slide past each other
The particles shake harder and harder
a: The particles shake a little on the spot
The particles shake harder and harder
Particles at the surface break out of their places
The particles slide past each other
items.why: Warming makes the particles shake harder. At the melting point the ones at the surface break free first, and then the whole solid becomes a liquid.

items.p: The ghee is hard in the morning and soft by afternoon. Nobody touched it. Explain why.
items.a: The morning was cooler than the melting points of the fats in ghee, so they were solid. The afternoon was warmer, so some or all of them melted.
items.why: A strong answer compares the temperature of the room with the melting point. It may add that ghee is a mixture and softens bit by bit.

items.p: Draw the particles of wax as a solid and as a liquid. Show how they move.
items.a: Solid: circles touching in neat rows, with small shake marks. Liquid: circles still touching but jumbled, with short arrows showing them sliding past each other.
items.why: A strong drawing keeps the particles the same size and close together in both. Only the order and the movement change.
items.art: Two large empty circles side by side, labelled solid wax and liquid wax.

items.p: You want to know if salt makes ice melt faster. What would you keep the same, and what would you measure?
items.a: Keep the same: the number and size of ice cubes, the bowls, the place and the time. Change only the salt. Measure the meltwater in teaspoons.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing only and names something that can be counted or measured.

worksheets.title: Hidden heat, salt and what comes back

items.p: Ice and water are stirred in a tumbler in a warm room. What does a thermometer show while ice is left?
items.why: About 0. The heat coming in is used to melt the ice, so the temperature holds at the melting point. A steady rise begins only when the ice has gone.

items.p: What is the heat that goes into melting ice used for?
opts: Pulling particles out of their places
items.why: The heat pulls the particles out of their fixed places against the pulls between them. The particles do not change in size or weight.

items.p: Why does a bowl of salted ice get colder than a bowl of plain ice?
opts: Salt is cold when it leaves the shelf
The extra melting takes heat from the ice and bowl
Salt keeps the room's heat out
items.why: Salt makes more ice melt, and melting takes in heat. With no one heating the bowl, the heat comes from the ice, the bowl and the salty water. Salt on the shelf is at room temperature.

items.p: A spoon of sugar melts less ice than a spoon of salt. What is the main reason?
opts: A spoon of sugar has far fewer particles
items.why: What matters most is how many dissolved particles get in the way at the surface of the ice. Sugar particles are big, so a spoonful holds about ten times fewer.

items.p: Ghee melts bit by bit and not at one temperature. Why?
opts: It is a mixture of many fats
It has been kept too long
items.why: Each fat in ghee has its own melting point. The low ones melt first and the high ones last, so ghee softens over a stretch of temperatures.

items.p: True or false: a sealed bottle of ice gets lighter when the ice melts.
items.why: False. Nothing leaves the sealed bottle, so the weight is the same. Try it on a kitchen scale.

items.p: True or false: a piece of bronze glowing red at 900 degrees can be a frozen solid.
items.why: True. Bronze turns solid a little below 1,000 degrees. At 900 it is below its freezing point, so it is solid, even though it glows.

items.p: Water that is colder than 0 degrees but still liquid is called ____ water.
items.why: Supercooled water has not yet started to freeze, because no seed of ice has formed in it.

items.p: Salt dissolved in water makes the freezing point of the water ____.
items.why: Salty water freezes below 0 degrees. Sea water freezes at about minus 2.

items.p: Match each thing to what it does.
pairs: Salt on a kulfi seller's ice
makes the ice mix colder than 0 degrees
stays at 0 degrees while any ice is left
items.why: Each one uses a melting point: lowering it with salt, holding steady at it, going above it, or going below it.

items.p: A wax figure is melted and the wax sets again. Sort what comes back and what does not.
cats: Does not come back by itself
items: Does not come back by itself
the fine lines on the surface
Does not come back by itself
items.why: Melting is reversible for the substance and its amount. The form is lost, and has to be made again with a mould or with hands.

items.p: Put these in order from the lowest melting point to the highest.
items.why: Mercury minus 39, ice 0, coconut oil about 24, candle wax about 60, iron 1,538. Mercury is liquid in a room, so its melting point must be below room temperature.

items.p: Fish sellers pack fish in crushed ice, not in cold water. Use hidden heat to explain why ice is better.
items.a: Melting ice takes in a lot of heat and stays at 0 degrees until it has all melted. Cold water has no ice to melt, so the same heat warms it up quickly.
items.why: A strong answer says the ice stays at 0 while it melts, and that melting takes in far more heat than warming water by a few degrees.

items.p: Three people are talking about a glass window.

views.says: Glass is a liquid that flows too slowly to see.
Glass is a solid. It keeps its shape and it breaks.
It depends on how long you watch.

items.ask: Which view do you find strongest? Give a reason. Then say what evidence would change your mind.
items.a: Any view can be defended. A strong answer gives evidence, such as glass keeping its shape for 2,000 years, or its particles being jumbled like a liquid's, and names something that would change the writer's mind.
items.why: The second view fits what we can measure in a human lifetime. The first is right that the particles are jumbled, but old windows have not flowed. The third is the one physicists use for pitch and tar. Whether glass is a true state of matter is still argued.

items.p: A friend says salt is warm, and that is why it melts ice. What test would show her it is not so?
items.a: Touch the outside of a bowl of salted ice and a bowl of plain ice, or put a thermometer in each. The salted one is colder.
items.why: A strong answer names something to feel or measure, and compares the salted ice with plain ice.

worksheets.title: The edges: supercooling, glass, pressure and proof

items.p: A clean bottle of water is at minus 5 degrees and still liquid. What does it need in order to freeze?
opts: A seed, from a speck or a knock
items.why: It is already cold enough. It needs a first group of particles in the pattern of ice. A speck, a scratch or a knock helps one to form.

items.p: Supercooled water flash-freezes into slush, not a hard block. Why?
opts: Freezing gives out heat, which warms it back to 0
items.why: As ice forms it gives out hidden heat. This warms the water back up to 0 degrees, and then no more can freeze until the freezer takes that heat away.

items.p: The Earth's inner core is solid iron at more than 5,000 degrees. What keeps it solid?
items.why: Pressure raises the melting point of iron. At the centre of the Earth the pressure is millions of times that of the air, so iron stays solid far above 1,538 degrees.

items.p: A tiny speck of gold melts at a lower temperature than a gold bangle. Why?
opts: Most of its particles are at the surface
The speck is not real gold
items.why: Particles at a surface have fewer neighbours holding them, so they break free more easily. In a tiny speck, most particles are at the surface.

items.p: You want to mark 0 degrees on a new thermometer. Which would you trust more?
opts: Still water in a freezer, as it freezes
items.why: Melting ice always holds 0 degrees. Still water can go below 0 before it freezes, so the moment of freezing is not a dependable mark.

items.p: True or false: camphor left in an open tin turns into a liquid first, and then into a gas.
items.why: False. In the open air camphor goes straight from solid to gas and leaves no puddle. This is called sublimation.

items.p: True or false: water always turns to ice as soon as it is cooled to 0 degrees.
items.why: False. Clean, still water can stay liquid below 0. It freezes only when a seed of ice forms.

items.p: A solid turning straight into a gas, with no liquid in between, is called ____.
items.why: Camphor, naphthalene balls and dry ice all do this in the open air.

items.p: Ice takes up ____ room than the water it was made from.
items.why: In ice the particles lock into open rings, which take up more room. That is why ice cubes have a bump and why ice floats.

items.p: Match each scientist to what they found.
pairs: water can stay liquid below its freezing point
the Earth has a solid inner core
old window glass has not flowed
sugar may break down before it melts
items.why: Each finding showed that a simple statement about melting or freezing needed a closer look.

items.p: Sort these: does it melt at one exact temperature, or soften over a stretch?
items.why: Pure substances with particles in neat rows melt at a point. Mixtures such as ghee and chocolate, and glass with its jumbled particles, soften over a stretch.

items.p: Put the steps of casting a bronze figure in order.
items: Pour melted bronze into the hollow
Break the clay when the bronze has set
Heat the mould so that the wax runs out
Coat the wax in clay and let it dry
a: Coat the wax in clay and let it dry
Heat the mould so that the wax runs out
Pour melted bronze into the hollow
Break the clay when the bronze has set
items.why: The wax melts at about 60 degrees and leaves a hollow. The bronze, melted at about 1,000 degrees, fills the hollow and solidifies in the shape the wax had.

items.p: Is an ice cube sitting in ice-cold water doing nothing? Use particles to explain your answer.
items.a: No. Particles keep leaving the ice and others keep joining it. At 0 degrees the two happen equally fast, so the cube stays the same size.
items.why: A strong answer says that leaving and joining go on all the time, and that the cube looks still because they are in balance.

items.p: Draw a graph of temperature against time for ice at minus 10 warming until it is water at 20 degrees.
items.a: The line rises from minus 10 to 0, runs flat at 0 while the ice melts, then rises again to 20.
items.why: A strong graph has a flat stretch at 0 degrees. The heat going in there is melting the ice, not warming it.
items.art: Empty graph axes on squared paper, with time along the bottom and temperature from minus 10 to 20 up the side.

items.p: Two food scientists disagree about heating table sugar.

views.says: Sugar starts to break down into new substances before it melts. It has no true melting point.
Sugar does melt, at about 186 degrees. It also breaks down at the same time.

items.ask: What test could help to decide between them? Say what each scientist would expect to see.
items.a: One good test is to heat sugar quickly and slowly and compare the temperature at which it turns liquid. Another is to cool the liquid and check whether it is still only sugar. A strong answer says what each side predicts.
items.why: A true melting point should not depend on how fast you heat, which is the evidence on one side. If the cooled liquid were still pure sugar, that would support the other. Food scientists have not settled this.

quiz.p: Melted bronze cools from 1,100 degrees to 900 and turns solid. What is this change called?
quiz.why: A liquid turning solid is freezing, at any temperature. If you chose melting, think about which way the change went: from liquid to solid.

quiz.p: Pure water can freeze at 0 degrees. At what temperature does pure ice melt?
quiz.why: For a pure substance the melting point and the freezing point are the same temperature. 100 degrees is where water boils.

quiz.p: What do the particles of a solid do at its melting point?
opts: Break out of their places and slide past each other
quiz.why: The particles shake hard enough to break out of their places. They never stop moving, and they do not split. They are the same particles in the liquid.

quiz.p: True or false: when ice melts, each water particle melts too.
quiz.why: False. One particle cannot be solid or liquid. Melting is a change in how the particles are arranged and how they move.

quiz.p: Coconut oil melts at about 24 degrees. On which kitchen shelf is it solid?
quiz.why: Only 8 degrees is below the melting point of 24. In Chennai and Kochi the shelf is warmer than 24, so the oil is liquid.

quiz.p: Mustard oil stays liquid through a Delhi winter. What does this tell you about its melting point?
opts: It is below the winter temperature
quiz.why: A substance is liquid when it is warmer than its melting point. So the melting point of mustard oil must be lower than a Delhi winter day.

quiz.p: A tumbler of ice and water stands in the sun. Half the ice has gone. How warm is the water, if stirred?
quiz.why: While any ice is left, the heat from the sun goes into melting it. The stirred water stays at about 0 degrees.

quiz.p: You stir salt into a bowl of ice. What happens?
opts: It melts faster and gets colder
It melts faster and gets warmer
It melts more slowly and gets colder
quiz.why: Salt tips the balance towards melting, and melting takes in heat from the ice and the bowl. If you chose warmer, remember that salt gives no heat.

quiz.p: Why does a kulfi seller mix salt into the ice around the kulfi?
opts: To make the ice mix colder than 0 degrees
To stop the ice from melting
quiz.why: Sweet milk freezes below 0 degrees, and plain ice is only at 0. Ice with salt can reach minus 15, which is cold enough. The salt makes the ice melt faster, not slower.

quiz.p: A goldsmith melts a ring and casts a coin from it. What is the same before and after?
quiz.why: Melting and solidifying are reversible. The gold and its weight are unchanged. The shape is new, because the liquid took the shape of the mould.

quiz.p: Which sentence about window glass is true?
opts: It softens slowly, with no exact melting point
It melts at one exact temperature
It has flowed down in old windows
quiz.why: The particles of glass are jumbled, so it softens over a stretch of temperatures. Careful sums show old panes have not flowed. They were made uneven.

quiz.p: True or false: scientists fully agree on how melting first starts inside a solid.
quiz.why: False. They agree on what melting is, but how the very first particles break free is still being studied.

quiz.p: In a fair test of salt on ice, what is the only thing that should change?
opts: What is sprinkled on the ice
quiz.why: If the bowls or the number of cubes changed too, you could not tell what caused the difference. Change one thing and keep the rest the same.

quiz.p: Your test gave 8 spoons of meltwater for salt and 3 for plain ice, once. What should you do next?
opts: Change the numbers to look neater
quiz.why: One try can be a fluke. If a second try gives nearly the same result, you can trust it more. Results are never changed to look neater.

applications: Casting: bronze figures, steel machine parts, gold ornaments and candles are all made by melting a substance, pouring it into a mould and letting it solidify.
Using things again: steel, aluminium, glass, gold and wax can be melted and made into new objects, because melting is a reversible change.
Keeping things cold: fish, medicines and vaccines travel in melting ice, which holds a steady 0 degrees for hours.
Making kulfi and ice cream with ice and salt, which gets far colder than ice alone.
Clearing icy roads and runways in cold places with salt.
Setting thermometers: the world's temperature scale is fixed by the melting and freezing points of pure substances.
Joining wires: solder is a metal mixture that melts at about 200 degrees, so it can join parts without melting them.
Safety fuses: a thin wire in a fuse melts and breaks the path when too much electricity flows.
Checking purity: chemists test a medicine by its melting point, because an impure sample melts lower and over a wider stretch.

open_questions.q: How exactly does melting begin inside a solid?
open_questions.why_open: The first steps involve a few particles and last less than a millionth of a second. Rules such as Lindemann's from 1910 give roughly the right temperature but do not describe what happens. New cameras that use flashes of electrons are only now starting to catch it.

open_questions.q: Is glass a true state of matter, or a liquid that has become too slow to move?
open_questions.why_open: To find out, a liquid would have to be cooled so slowly that the test would take longer than a human life. The physicist Philip Anderson wrote in 1995 that this may be the deepest unsolved problem in the science of solids. It is still unsolved.

open_questions.q: Can anyone say exactly when a bottle of supercooled water will freeze?
open_questions.why_open: The first seed of ice forms by chance among a few hundred particles. Scientists can give the odds, but not the moment. They also do not fully know how the proteins of some bacteria arrange water into a seed so well.

open_questions.q: Does very cold water come in two different liquid forms?
open_questions.why_open: The place to look is near minus 70 degrees, where water freezes in less than a thousandth of a second. Only a few experiments, with very fast X-ray flashes, have reached it, and scientists read the results differently.

open_questions.q: At what temperature does the iron at the centre of the Earth melt?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody can go there, and the pressure is very hard to copy in a laboratory. Different experiments give answers that differ by about a thousand degrees.

maths.context: This is about the melting points you met in this lesson.
maths.problem: Put these melting points in order from the coldest to the hottest: 24, minus 39, 0, 60, minus 210, 30.
maths.explain: Numbers below 0 come first, and the one furthest below 0 is the coldest. So minus 210 is colder than minus 39. Then come 0, 24, 30 and 60. These are nitrogen, mercury, ice, coconut oil, gallium and candle wax.
maths.why_maths: Many melting points are below 0, so you need numbers less than 0 to put them in order.

maths.context: This is about coconut oil on a kitchen shelf.
maths.problem: Coconut oil melts at 24 degrees. At 7 in the morning the shelf is at 19 degrees. At 2 in the afternoon it is at 31. How many degrees below the melting point is the morning? How many above is the afternoon?
maths.answer: 5 degrees below in the morning. 7 degrees above in the afternoon.
maths.explain: 24 minus 19 is 5, so the morning is 5 degrees below and the oil is solid. 31 minus 24 is 7, so the afternoon is 7 degrees above and the oil is liquid.
maths.why_maths: Whether a substance is solid or liquid depends on the difference between its temperature and its melting point.

maths.context: This is about the Salt Test, with made-up numbers.
maths.problem: In a Salt Test the plain bowl gave 3 teaspoons of meltwater, the sugar bowl 4 and the salt bowl 9. How many times as much as the plain bowl did the salt bowl give? Each bowl started with ice worth 12 teaspoons. What fraction of the salted ice melted?
maths.answer: 3 times as much. Three quarters of the salted ice melted.
maths.explain: 9 divided by 3 is 3, so the salt bowl gave 3 times as much. 9 out of 12 is the same as 3 out of 4, which is three quarters.
maths.why_maths: Saying '3 times as much' and 'three quarters' lets you compare your result with another family's, even if their ice cubes were a different size.

maths.context: This is about the Flat Line test, with made-up readings.
maths.problem: Tumbler B, with cold water only, read 8, 10, 11, 13, 14 and 15 degrees at 0, 3, 6, 9, 12 and 15 minutes. Tumbler A, with ice, read 1, 0, 0, 0, 0 and 0. How many degrees did B warm in 15 minutes? How many did A warm? What does the line for A look like on a graph?
maths.answer: B warmed by 7 degrees. A did not warm at all, and in fact fell by 1. The line for A is flat along 0.
maths.explain: 15 minus 8 is 7. A went from 1 to 0 and stayed there. On a graph, B is a line going up and A is a flat line along 0, because the heat going into A was melting ice.
maths.why_maths: A line graph shows at a glance what a table hides: one line climbs and the other stays flat.

chart.title: Made-up readings for tumbler B, cold water only

maths.context: This is about a real experiment in Australia, where a lump of pitch has been dripping slowly through a funnel since 1930.
maths.problem: The funnel of pitch was opened in 1930. Drops fell in 1938, 1947, 1954, 1962, 1970, 1979, 1988, 2000 and 2014. How many years passed from 1930 to the ninth drop? About how many years is that for each drop? Are the gaps getting longer or shorter?
maths.answer: 84 years. About 9 years for each drop. The last two gaps, 12 and 14 years, are the longest.
maths.explain: 2014 minus 1930 is 84. 84 divided by 9 is a little over 9. The gaps are 8, 9, 7, 8, 8, 9, 9, 12 and 14 years. The last two are longer, and the scientists think air conditioning put into the building made the pitch cooler and slower.
maths.why_maths: An average tells you how slowly the pitch flows, and looking at each gap shows that the average hides a change.

maths.problem: The heat that melts one ice cube could warm the same amount of water by 80 degrees. By how many degrees could that heat warm twice as much water? Four times as much?
maths.answer: 40 degrees for twice as much water. 20 degrees for four times as much.
maths.explain: The same heat shared among twice as much water warms it half as much. Half of 80 is 40. Shared among four times as much, it warms it a quarter as much. A quarter of 80 is 20.
maths.why_maths: This sum shows why a few ice cubes can cool a whole jug of water: melting takes in a great deal of heat.

roots.context: In the salt test, the salted ice melted fastest and its bowl became the coldest, though nobody heated it or cooled it. This part looks at what that shows about an ice cube that seems to be sitting still, and about you.

deep_truth.truth: In the salt test, the salted ice melted fastest and also became the coldest. Salt gave the ice no heat. At the surface of ice, particles leave and join all the time, and salt tipped that balance. So an ice cube that looks still is a balance between leaving and joining. A solid stays solid only while everything around it keeps that balance with it.
deep_truth.habit: We think 'solid' is something a thing has all by itself, the way it has a name. We also think a thing that looks still is doing nothing. The salt test questions both. The ice changed because of what touched it, and it was never still.
deep_truth.evidence: In the salt test, the bowl with salt gave the most meltwater and felt the coldest. In Ghee There and Back, the same spoon of ghee was liquid over warm water and solid over cold water within a few minutes. If your results were different, use what you saw.

three.who_am_i: Your body is at about 37 degrees. At that temperature the fats in the thin skins of your cells are just soft enough to bend and let things through, and your bones are far below their melting point. You are a balance of solids and liquids, held steady every second. You do not hold it alone. The air, your food and the Sun's warmth keep it with you.
three.what_is_life: Living beings do not just put up with melting points. They sense the cold and change themselves. When the water cools, fish and bacteria change the fats in their cell skins so that these stay soft. Wood frogs let ice form between their cells in winter and thaw alive in spring. Bacteria on leaves build seeds for ice.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth sits at a temperature where water is ice on the Himalaya, liquid in the Kaveri and vapour in the monsoon cloud, all at once. A little warmer or a little cooler, and one of the three would be missing. The Ganga and the Indus are fed by melting ice and snow. What we call the world's solid things and flowing things are one set of particles, sorted by warmth.

roots.thread: The lesson began with coconut oil that is solid in the morning and liquid by lunch. Then salt, which is not warm, melted ice. Then water stayed liquid below zero until something gave it a start. In each case the substance alone did not decide what it was. The warmth of the room, what was dissolved in it, a speck of dust and how long we watched all took part. Solid and liquid are things a substance does together with its surroundings.

teachings.teaching: The Vaisheshika thinkers taught that ghee, lac and beeswax, and also tin, lead, iron, silver and gold, become fluid through contact with fire. They taught that this flowing is caused from outside and is not the solid's own nature. Scholars do not agree on the date of the text.
teachings.link: In Ghee There and Back, the ghee flowed only while the warm water was under it. Take the warmth away and it set. Its flowing depended on what it touched.

teachings.teaching: The teacher Uddalaka tells his son Shvetaketu that by knowing one lump of gold, everything made of gold is known. The bangle and the ring are names given in speech. What is real in them, he says, is the gold.
teachings.link: A goldsmith melts a bangle and casts a ring, and the gold is the same gold. Melting and solidifying show what stays when the form changes. Uddalaka uses this to point at one reality under all forms.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha taught: when this is, that is. From the arising of this, that arises. Nothing stands by itself. Each thing is there because of the conditions around it.
teachings.link: The ice in your bowl was solid because the freezer had been cold. It melted because the room was warm, and it melted faster because salt was there. Change the conditions and the ice changes.

science.text: At the melting point, particles leave the solid and join it at equal rates. A solid that sits unchanged in its own liquid is a two-way exchange in balance.
Dissolved particles lower the freezing point of a liquid, and melting takes in heat from the surroundings.
How melting first begins inside a solid, particle by particle, is not fully worked out.
Whether glass is a true state of matter or a liquid that has become too slow to move is argued among physicists.
Consciousness is the ground from which particles and their balances arise. Science has no test for this yet, and many scientists hold that particles come first and minds arise later, only in brains.

other_view.who: Most chemists, and the Vaisheshika thinkers themselves
other_view.view: A melting point belongs to the substance. Pure water has the same one in every laboratory on Earth, which is why thermometers are set by it. On this view the world is made of many separate things, each with its own fixed properties. The 'balance' is only a count of separate particles bumping into each other. Nothing in the salt test needs the idea that things are one.

practice.title: Ice on the palm
practice.say: Hold one ice cube on your open palm over a bowl. Close your eyes. Notice the cold spreading into your hand. The ice is taking heat from you to melt. Take three slow breaths. Now ask yourself where your hand got that heat from. Put the ice in the bowl and dry your hand.
practice.kid: Hold an ice cube on your palm over a bowl. Close your eyes and take three slow breaths. Your hand is giving heat to the ice. Where did your hand get that heat?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project here was worked through step by step against what is known to happen in a home kitchen, but has not yet been run by a family. The Salt Test uses 12 ice cubes, three small steel bowls and a teaspoon each of salt and sugar. In a room near 29 degrees, plain ice usually gives 2 to 4 teaspoons of meltwater in 15 minutes and salted ice about twice that or more. Sugar comes out close to plain, sometimes a little above. In a cool room, wait 25 minutes. The Flat Line test needs a kitchen thermometer that reads below 0. Stirred ice water stays within a degree of 0, and two teaspoons of salt usually take it to between minus 2 and minus 6. Flash Freeze depends on the freezer and works about one time in three, which the steps say. The Kulfi Maker's Trick needs two full trays of ice, and the milk in the salted bowl freezes on the wall of the tumbler in about 10 minutes. Dip or Bump shows the ice rising clearly and the oil sinking only a little. Free the Coin needs the coins frozen the day before. The Melting Point Ladder was played through with two and with four players, and ends when the pile is empty.
